transcript.content:
It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the astronomical data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with the naked eye right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Contrast)
The biggest factor here is the **Sun's altitude (59.542 degrees)**. Because the Sun is very high in the sky and it is "bright daylight," the atmosphere is filled with scattered sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high level of background luminance. For an object to be visible to the human eye, it must be significantly brighter than the background it is sitting against.

### 2. The Moon's Phase (Illumination)
You noted the Moon is only **2.74% illuminated**. This means you are looking at a very thin crescent. While a Full Moon is bright enough to punch through daylight, a 2.7% crescent lacks the surface area to reflect enough sunlight to compete with the brightness of a clear, sunny sky.

### 3. Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only **19.022 degrees from the Sun**. In observational astronomy, this is very close. When an object is that close to the Sun in the sky, it is often lost in the "glare" or the general brightness of the solar neighborhood. It’s similar to trying to see a dim lightbulb while someone is pointing a high-powered flashlight nearby.

### 4. Visual Comparison
Imagine trying to see a tiny, dim candle flame while standing in the middle of a brightly lit stadium during the day. Even if the candle is "there," your pupils will constrict to adjust to the overwhelming brightness of the sun, making the faint light of a tiny crescent Moon virtually invisible.

**Verdict:**
Unless you have high-powered binoculars or a telescope to "isolate" the Moon from the rest of the sky, **it will be effectively invisible to your unaided eyes.** You can relax—the Moon is there, but it isn't "showing up" in the daylight.
